boundary_note: Bounded first pass for the frozen Buck Head Creek record (November 28, 1864) in the Savannah Campaign [November-December 1864]. Wheeler's night attack of November 26-27 and the fighting near Waynesborough on the 27th precede it; Waynesborough (GA027) follows on December 4. Campaign-wide marches, returns, reinforcements and multi-action loss totals are context; they are not assigned to one record or added across records. Draft claims do not alter model inputs.

claims.rationale: No inspected return establishes matched personnel at a common opening boundary. The frozen side-specific numerical strength bounds are blank (missing_numeric_strength). No figure in this pass is adopted as a simultaneous opening force.

claims.value: The frozen force text names Kilpatrick's 3rd Cavalry Division against the cavalry corps of the department, with no numbers; the live field reads zeros. Kilpatrick says he left Marietta on November 14 with 5,500 men and six guns in two brigades of 2,800 and 2,700. Wheeler says only about 1,200 of his command had crossed the creek when he attacked the barricades, that his force never exceeded 3,500 and he seldom had more than 2,000 under his immediate command, and that the enemy's cavalry was at least double his own numbers.
claims.rationale: Kilpatrick's figures are for November 14; Wheeler's are campaign-wide claims and a partial count at the creek. None is adopted as a matched opening strength; live zeros are not measured absence.

claims.value: Wheeler says an intervening swamp at Buck Head Creek made approach almost impossible and saved Kilpatrick, that the bridge had been prepared for burning, and that beyond it the open ground ended at a line cavalry could not approach. Kilpatrick says he took a strong position two miles beyond the creek behind a long line of barricades with his flanks thrown back. NPS says a Union brigade behind barricades at Reynolds's Plantation halted the drive.
claims.rationale: The creek and swamp predate the action; the barricades were built during it.

Wheeler says Kilpatrick was very nearly captured, that he sent Dibrell and Ashby to turn the flanks, and that Ashby took the wrong road by accident. The frozen commanders are Major General Wheeler and Brigadier General H. Judson Kilpatrick; the live page lists 'Hugh Kilpatrick'.

claims.value: The frozen result reads Union victory; the live result reads Indecisive. Kilpatrick says Wheeler was 'most handsomely repulsed at all points'; Wheeler says his charge sent the enemy fleeing in uncontrollable confusion and that the rout was complete. NPS says the barricades eventually forced Wheeler to retire.
claims.rationale: Retain the original result and engagement interval; later movements and campaign contribution are different measures. No new probabilities or individual causal credit. The frozen and live result fields and the commanders' characterizations conflict.

claims.value: The frozen and live casualty fields read 646 (US 46; CS 600). Kilpatrick says his losses over three days were not large and estimates the enemy's at 600 killed and wounded; his campaign total, November 14-December, is 1 officer killed, 6 wounded and 2 missing and 31 men killed, 153 wounded and 166 missing. Wheeler claims nearly 200 captured, killed and wounded in the charge before the creek.
claims.rationale: Original casualty returns were not inspected; preserve totals, categories, cutoffs and differences. No canonical reconciliation or casualty-based opening count; related actions must not be added without resolving population overlap. Kilpatrick's 600 is an estimate for three days of fighting; his campaign total is context and is not assigned to this record.

open_questions: Murray's No. 144, Atkins's No. 150, Heath's No. 153 and the other regimental reports, Kilpatrick's nominal casualty list, Dibrell's, Humes's and Ashby's reports, and Cox's Buck Head Creek passage (pp.32–33, read, not selected) remain deferred.

NPS/CWSAC (the live NPS page and the frozen Arnold rows) is one family. C. R. Woods's, G. W. Smith's, Kilpatrick's, Wheeler's, J. P. Hatch's and Hazen's reports, printed in Official Records Series I, Volume XLIV, are separate families of interested commanders' accounts; the volume is a shared container, not an additional witness. Jacob D. Cox's The March to the Sea; Franklin and Nashville (1882) is a later history drawing on the official papers; Cox was not in this campaign. Report dates are not event times or proof of contemporary knowledge.
No automatic commander attribution, causal campaign score, morale/readiness number or battle/campaign double counting.
